postgresql: In PostgreSQL, what happens to the old version of a row when you UPDATE it?
It is kept as a dead tuple until VACUUM reclaims it
It is overwritten in place inside the same data page
It is copied into a separate rollback segment file
It is physically deleted the moment the transaction commits
PostgreSQL MVCC writes a new row version and leaves the old one as a dead tuple. Unlike Oracle or InnoDB, there is no undo log; VACUUM later reclaims the space.
In PostgreSQL at the default READ COMMITTED level, what does a SELECT see if another transaction has updated a row but not committed yet?
The last committed version of the row
The uncommitted new version of the row
Nothing, the SELECT waits until the other commits
A serialization failure error is raised
MVCC gives each statement a snapshot of committed data, so readers never block on writers and never see dirty data. PostgreSQL does not allow dirty reads at any level.
Which PostgreSQL index type is the usual choice for speeding up the @> containment operator on a JSONB column?
GIN
B-Tree
BRIN
Hash
GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes the keys and values inside a JSONB document, which is what @>, ? and ?| need. A B-Tree only compares whole values.
A huge append-only PostgreSQL table stores events whose created_at value grows with the physical row order. Which index type gives tiny size and good range filtering on created_at?
BRIN
GIN
GiST
Hash
BRIN stores min and max values per block range, so it is extremely small and works well when the column correlates with physical order.
Which PostgreSQL index type supports an exclusion constraint that prevents overlapping booking time ranges (the && operator on tstzrange)?
GiST
B-Tree
BRIN
Hash
GiST supports range and geometric operators such as && (overlaps), so EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&) is the standard pattern. A B-Tree only handles equality and ordering.
What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE do differently from plain EXPLAIN in PostgreSQL?
It executes the query and reports real timings and row counts
It shows estimated costs only, without running the query
It rewrites the query into a faster equivalent form
It refreshes table statistics before showing the plan
EXPLAIN only shows the planner's estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the statement and adds actual time, actual rows and loops to each plan node.
In EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, a scan node estimated rows=10 but the actual rows were 250000. What is the most likely first fix?
Run ANALYZE on the table to refresh planner statistics
Run VACUUM FULL to rebuild the table and its indexes
Increase work_mem for the session running the query
Drop and recreate the primary key to reset the index
A large gap between estimated and actual rows usually means stale or missing statistics. ANALYZE recollects them so the planner can choose a better plan.
Why should you be careful running EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2020-01-01' in PostgreSQL?
The DELETE really runs and removes the rows
It locks the whole database for writes
It disables autovacuum on the table
It drops the indexes that it uses
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. To inspect a data-modifying plan safely, wrap it in BEGIN and ROLLBACK.
What does a plain VACUUM (without FULL) do in PostgreSQL?
Marks dead-tuple space reusable without blocking reads or writes
Rewrites the table into a new file and returns the freed space to the OS
Rebuilds every index on the table from scratch
Deletes rows older than the autovacuum threshold
Plain VACUUM records freed space in the free space map for reuse and runs alongside normal traffic. Returning space to the OS by rewriting the table is what VACUUM FULL does.
What is the main operational drawback of VACUUM FULL on a busy PostgreSQL table?
It takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking reads and writes
It cannot return freed disk space to the operating system at all
It only works on tables that have no indexes defined
It can only run while autovacuum is turned off
VACUUM FULL rewrites the whole table into a new file, which needs an exclusive lock for the duration. Tools like pg_repack are used to avoid this downtime.
Why must autovacuum not be disabled permanently on a PostgreSQL database with heavy writes?
Vacuum freezes old rows to prevent transaction ID wraparound
Vacuum is what moves committed data from the WAL into the tables
Vacuum is required before new foreign keys can be added
Vacuum is what rotates and compresses the server logs
Transaction IDs are 32-bit, so old rows must be frozen. Without vacuuming, PostgreSQL eventually stops accepting writes to protect against wraparound.
In PostgreSQL, what does SELECT '{"a": {"b": 5}}'::jsonb -> 'a' ->> 'b' return?
5 as text
5 as jsonb
{"b": 5} as jsonb
NULL as text
The -> operator returns jsonb (the inner object), and ->> returns the selected value as text.
Which statement about jsonb compared with json in PostgreSQL is true?
jsonb stores a parsed binary form and keeps only the last duplicate key
jsonb preserves key order and whitespace exactly as they were entered
jsonb cannot be indexed with GIN, unlike the plain json type
jsonb only accepts top-level objects, never arrays or scalars
jsonb is decomposed on input, so it drops whitespace, does not keep key order and keeps only the last value of a duplicate key. In return it is faster to query and supports GIN indexes.
A PostgreSQL table uses PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at). What lets a query with WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01' skip irrelevant partitions?
Partition pruning
Index-only scans
Parallel sequential scans
Deferred constraint checking
Partition pruning compares the WHERE clause with each partition's bounds and excludes partitions that cannot contain matching rows, at plan time or at execution time.
In PostgreSQL 11 or later, you insert a row into a range-partitioned table, but its key matches no partition and there is no DEFAULT partition. What happens?
The INSERT fails with an error
The row goes into the last partition
A new partition is created automatically
The row is stored in the parent table
PostgreSQL raises an error that no partition was found for the row. A DEFAULT partition, added in version 11, can catch such rows.
You want a primary key on a partitioned PostgreSQL table partitioned by created_at. What must the key include?
The partition key column created_at
Only a serial or identity column as the key
A hash index on all columns
Nothing extra, any columns work
Unique constraints on partitioned tables must include all partition key columns, because each partition enforces uniqueness only locally.
What is the main purpose of PostgreSQL's Write-Ahead Log (WAL)?
Logging changes first so the database can recover after a crash
Caching query results so that repeated reads are faster
Storing old row versions that MVCC snapshots read from
Recording slow statements so they can be tuned later
Changes are written to WAL before data pages are flushed, so after a crash PostgreSQL replays WAL to a consistent state. WAL also feeds streaming replication and point-in-time recovery.
Which PostgreSQL replication type can copy only selected tables to a server running a different major version?
Logical replication
Physical replication
WAL file shipping
Hot standby replication

Logical replication sends row changes through publications and subscriptions, so it works per table and across major versions. Physical replication copies the whole cluster byte for byte and needs the same major version.
Table orders has customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. What happens when you delete a customer in PostgreSQL?
That customer's orders are deleted too
Their orders get customer_id set to NULL
The delete fails if the customer has orders
The orders keep a dangling customer_id
ON DELETE CASCADE removes referencing rows automatically. SET NULL is a different action, and the default NO ACTION would make the delete fail.
You add a foreign key on orders.customer_id referencing customers(id) in PostgreSQL. Which index is created automatically on orders.customer_id?
None; add one yourself if needed
A B-Tree index on orders.customer_id
A hash index on orders.customer_id
A unique index on orders.customer_id
PostgreSQL requires a unique index on the referenced columns but never indexes the referencing column automatically. Without it, deletes on customers and joins can be slow.
mysql: Which storage engine is the default in MySQL 5.5 and later?
InnoDB
MyISAM
MEMORY
CSV
InnoDB became the default in MySQL 5.5 because it supports transactions, row-level locking and crash recovery.
Which feature does InnoDB provide that MyISAM does not?
Transactions with COMMIT and ROLLBACK
Full-text search indexes on text columns
Compressed read-only tables with myisampack
A stored row count for instant COUNT(*)
MyISAM is non-transactional. Both engines support full-text indexes (InnoDB since 5.6), while myisampack and the stored row count are MyISAM features.
What locking granularity does MyISAM use for writes?
Table-level locks
Row-level locks
Page-level locks
Column-level locks
MyISAM locks the whole table for each write, so concurrent writes serialize. InnoDB uses row-level locks instead.
In InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ, what does SELECT ... WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE lock?
Next-key locks on the scanned index range
The entire table for the transaction
Nothing, it reads a consistent snapshot
Only rows that already exist, no gaps
InnoDB uses next-key locks (record plus gap locks) so other transactions cannot insert phantom rows into the locked range.
Two InnoDB transactions each hold a row lock that the other one needs. What does InnoDB do by default?
Detects the deadlock and rolls back one transaction
Waits forever until an admin kills one
Commits both transactions in arbitrary order after a timeout
Escalates both row locks to a table lock
InnoDB deadlock detection is on by default. It picks a victim, rolls it back and returns error 1213 so the application can retry.
Which MySQL binlog_format always logs the actual changed rows instead of SQL statements?
ROW
STATEMENT
MIXED
DYNAMIC
ROW logs row images for every change. MIXED switches between statement and row logging, and DYNAMIC is an InnoDB row format, not a binlog format.
What does semisynchronous replication add to default asynchronous MySQL replication?
Commit waits until a replica confirms it received the events
Replicas apply events in parallel using many threads
Replicas accept writes and sync them back to the source
The binlog is compressed before being sent
With semisync, the source waits for at least one replica to acknowledge receipt before the commit returns, which reduces data loss on failover.
Why can statement-based replication produce different data on a replica for INSERT INTO t VALUES (UUID())?
UUID() is re-evaluated on the replica, giving another value
The replica rejects any statement that calls a function like UUID()
Statement events are applied in a random order
The replica truncates values longer than 32 chars
In STATEMENT format the SQL text is replayed, so nondeterministic functions like UUID() run again on the replica. MySQL marks such statements unsafe and MIXED switches them to row logging.
What does the InnoDB buffer pool cache in memory?
Table and index data pages
Parsed SQL statements and their plans
Final result sets of SELECT queries
Binary log events before they are sent
The buffer pool holds data and index pages so reads and writes avoid disk I/O. MySQL 8.0 removed the old query cache entirely.
A dedicated MySQL server with spare RAM shows many disk reads for hot InnoDB data. Which setting should you raise first?
innodb_buffer_pool_size
max_connections
sort_buffer_size
innodb_log_buffer_size
A larger buffer pool keeps more of the working set in memory. sort_buffer_size is per sort and the log buffer only stages redo log writes.
A table has a B-Tree index on (last_name, first_name). Under the leftmost-prefix rule, which WHERE clause cannot use it for a normal index lookup?
WHERE first_name = 'Ali'
WHERE last_name = 'Nur'
WHERE last_name IN ('Nur')
WHERE last_name LIKE 'Nu%'
A composite index is sorted by last_name first, so a lookup must start with last_name. A condition on first_name alone cannot seek into it (at best a skip scan or full index scan).
In MySQL EXPLAIN, what does 'Using index' in the Extra column mean?
The query was answered from the index alone, without reading rows
An index was created automatically for this query and then dropped again
The optimizer ignored all indexes and scanned the whole table
The index was used only for sorting, via a filesort pass
'Using index' means a covering index: every needed column is in the index, so InnoDB skips the lookup into the clustered index.
An index exists on created_at, but WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024 is slow. Which rewrite lets MySQL use the index?
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) >= 2024 AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) < 2025
WHERE DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m-%d') LIKE '2024-%'
WHERE CAST(created_at AS CHAR(10)) BETWEEN '2024' AND '2025'
Wrapping an indexed column in a function hides it from a normal range scan. A plain range on the raw column is sargable.
How are rows of an InnoDB table physically organized?
In a clustered index ordered by the primary key
In a heap file, in the order rows were inserted
In a hash table that is keyed by an internal row ID
In separate files on disk for each column
InnoDB stores rows inside the primary key B-Tree. Secondary indexes store the primary key value to find the row.
Which MySQL system variable sets the time threshold, in seconds, for logging a query to the slow query log?
long_query_time
slow_query_threshold
min_examined_row_limit
slow_query_log_time
Queries running longer than long_query_time are logged when slow_query_log is on. The other two real variables add filters, and slow_query_threshold does not exist.
Which tool bundled with MySQL summarizes a slow query log by grouping similar queries?
mysqldumpslow
mysqlcheck
mysqlbinlog
mysqlimport
mysqldumpslow abstracts literal values and groups similar statements with counts and times. mysqlbinlog reads binary logs, not the slow log.
What is the default transaction isolation level of InnoDB?
REPEATABLE READ
READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, unlike PostgreSQL and SQL Server which default to READ COMMITTED.
Which anomaly is possible for plain SELECTs in InnoDB at READ COMMITTED but not at REPEATABLE READ?
Non-repeatable reads
Reads of rolled-back data
Dirty writes on one row
Torn page writes
At READ COMMITTED each SELECT takes a fresh snapshot, so rereading a row can show another transaction's committed change. REPEATABLE READ reuses the first snapshot of the transaction.
With autocommit enabled (the MySQL default), what happens to an UPDATE run without START TRANSACTION?
It is committed immediately as its own transaction
It stays pending until you run COMMIT in that session
It is rolled back automatically when the session ends
It is queued until the next InnoDB checkpoint runs
With autocommit = 1, every statement outside an explicit transaction is its own transaction and commits on success.
In MySQL you run START TRANSACTION, an INSERT, then ALTER TABLE, then ROLLBACK. What happens to the INSERT?
It stays, since ALTER TABLE caused an implicit commit
It is rolled back together with the ALTER TABLE statement
It is rolled back, but the ALTER TABLE remains
The ROLLBACK fails with a syntax error
Most DDL statements in MySQL cause an implicit commit before they run, so the earlier INSERT is already committed when ROLLBACK runs.
sqlite: What does it mean that SQLite is serverless?
The app's process reads and writes the database file directly
It runs only inside cloud functions such as AWS Lambda or Workers
It uses a background daemon that starts on demand
It keeps all data in the browser's IndexedDB
SQLite is a library linked into the application. There is no separate server process; each connection opens the database file itself.
How is a complete SQLite database usually stored?
In a single ordinary file on disk
In a directory with one file per table
In shared memory that is lost at reboot
In files managed by a separate server
The whole database (tables, indexes, schema) lives in one cross-platform file, plus temporary journal or WAL files during writes.
Which journal mode does a new SQLite database use by default to guarantee atomic commits?
DELETE (rollback journal)
WAL (write-ahead log)
TRUNCATE (rollback journal)
MEMORY (in-RAM journal)
The default journal_mode is DELETE: a rollback journal is created for each write transaction and deleted on commit. WAL must be enabled explicitly.
A script runs 100000 INSERTs into SQLite with no BEGIN or COMMIT and is very slow. What is the most effective fix?
Wrap the inserts in a single transaction
Add an index on every column before inserting
Run VACUUM before inserting the rows
Change all column types to TEXT first
Without an explicit transaction, each INSERT is its own transaction with its own disk sync. One transaction around the batch makes it orders of magnitude faster.
In SQLite rollback journal mode, while a writer holds the EXCLUSIVE lock to commit, what can other connections do with the database?
They can neither read nor write it
They can still read the last committed data
They can write to other tables in the file
They can read pages from their own cache
The EXCLUSIVE lock covers the whole file, so readers and writers must wait. WAL mode removes this reader blocking.
Which SQLite result code means a connection could not get a lock before its busy timeout expired (the 'database is locked' error)?
SQLITE_BUSY
SQLITE_CORRUPT
SQLITE_FULL
SQLITE_MISMATCH
SQLITE_BUSY is returned when another connection holds a conflicting lock. A busy timeout makes SQLite retry for a while before returning it.
Why does the SQLite documentation warn against keeping a database file on a network filesystem such as NFS?
Their file locking is often unreliable and can corrupt data
SQLite cannot open files over 2 GB on a network
Network paths are not valid in connection strings
SQLite encrypts files differently when they are stored on network drives
SQLite relies on correct file locks from the OS. Many network filesystems implement locking poorly, so concurrent access can corrupt the database.
What is the main benefit of PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL in SQLite?
Readers and the writer no longer block each other
Several writers can commit to the database at the same time
The database no longer needs any extra files on disk
Commits no longer need to survive a crash
In WAL mode, writes are appended to a separate log while readers keep using their snapshot. There is still only one writer at a time.
Which extra files appear next to app.db while a SQLite database is open in WAL mode?
app.db-wal and app.db-shm
app.db-journal and app.db-lock
app.db-log and app.db-idx
app.db-tmp and app.db-bak
The -wal file holds new transactions and the -shm file is a shared-memory index used to coordinate readers. The -journal file belongs to rollback mode.
In SQLite WAL mode, which operation copies committed pages from the WAL file back into the main database file?
A checkpoint
A VACUUM
A REINDEX
A PRAGMA optimize
Checkpoints run automatically (by default when the WAL reaches about 1000 pages) or via PRAGMA wal_checkpoint, moving content into the main file.
You declared REFERENCES in SQLite, but deleting a parent row leaves orphaned child rows without any error. What is the most likely cause?
Foreign keys are off until PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
SQLite ignores the REFERENCES clause entirely
The child table was created WITHOUT ROWID
The parent table lacks an AUTOINCREMENT key
For backward compatibility SQLite does not enforce foreign keys by default. The pragma must be set on each new connection.
Which SQLite pragma sets how long a connection waits for a lock before returning SQLITE_BUSY?
busy_timeout
lock_timeout
wait_time
journal_timeout
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000 makes SQLite retry for up to 5 seconds. The other names are not SQLite pragmas.
Which SQLite pragma is commonly used by apps to record which schema migration has been applied?
user_version
schema_version
application_id
data_version
user_version is a free integer in the file header reserved for applications. schema_version is maintained by SQLite itself, and changing it manually can corrupt the database.
Which schema change can SQLite's ALTER TABLE perform directly?
Add a new column
Change a column's type
Add a CHECK constraint
Change the primary key
SQLite's ALTER TABLE supports RENAME TABLE, RENAME COLUMN, ADD COLUMN and (since 3.35) DROP COLUMN. Other changes need a table rebuild.
What is the recommended way to change a column's type in an existing SQLite table?
Create a new table, copy rows, drop old, rename new
Run ALTER TABLE t MODIFY COLUMN c INTEGER
Run ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c TYPE INTEGER
Run REINDEX after editing the declared type
SQLite has no ALTER COLUMN, so the documented procedure is to rebuild the table inside a transaction and recreate its indexes and triggers.
In an ordinary (non-STRICT) SQLite table with column age INTEGER, what happens when you insert the value 'abc'?
The text 'abc' is stored as-is
The insert fails with a type mismatch
The value 0 is stored instead
NULL is stored in its place
SQLite uses type affinity: it tries to convert 'abc' to an integer, cannot, and stores the text. STRICT tables (3.37+) would reject it.
Which use case is the best fit for SQLite?
Local storage for a mobile or desktop app
A web backend with thousands of concurrent writers
One database shared by servers in several regions
A central store written by many bank branches
SQLite shines as an embedded, zero-configuration store for one application. Heavy concurrent writes from many clients suit client/server databases better.
How many write transactions can be active at the same time on one SQLite database file?
Only one
One per table
One per CPU core
Unlimited
SQLite serializes writes for the whole file, even in WAL mode. Many readers can run, but only one writer at a time.
In SQLite WAL mode, a reader keeps a very old transaction open for hours while writes continue. What is the typical effect?
Checkpoints cannot finish, so the WAL file keeps growing
The writer is blocked until the reader finishes
The reader starts seeing uncommitted writes
The database falls back to rollback journal mode
A checkpoint cannot overwrite pages a reader still needs, so the WAL cannot be reset and grows. Readers never see uncommitted data.
What is the main risk of PRAGMA synchronous = OFF in SQLite?
Power loss can corrupt the database or lose recent commits
Foreign key constraints are no longer checked on writes
Readers can see uncommitted data from other writers
The database falls back from WAL to rollback mode
With synchronous OFF, SQLite hands data to the OS without waiting for it to reach disk. Writes are faster, but an OS crash or power loss can corrupt the file.
mongodb: What is BSON in MongoDB?
A binary-encoded serialization of JSON-like documents
A query language for filtering MongoDB collections
A compression format used on disk for collection data files
A schema language for validating JSON documents
MongoDB stores documents as BSON, which is fast to traverse and adds types that JSON lacks, such as Date, ObjectId and Decimal128.
Which of these types exists in BSON but not in plain JSON?
ObjectId
Boolean
Array
Null
BSON extends JSON with types like ObjectId, Date, Int64 and Decimal128. Boolean, array and null exist in JSON already.
What is the maximum size of a single BSON document in MongoDB?
16 MB
4 MB
64 MB
1 GB
The 16 MB limit prevents a single document from using excessive RAM or bandwidth. Larger files are stored with GridFS.
Which aggregation stage filters documents, similar to WHERE in SQL?
$match
$project
$group
$unwind
$match keeps only documents that match a query. $project reshapes fields, $group aggregates and $unwind expands arrays.
What does db.orders.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: "$status", n: { $sum: 1 } } }]) return?
One document per status value with its count
Every order with a new field n set to 1
The total number of orders as one number
Orders sorted by status in groups of one
$group with _id: "$status" creates one output document per distinct status, and $sum: 1 counts the documents in each group.
A document has tags: ["a", "b", "c"]. What does { $unwind: "$tags" } output for it?
Three documents, one per array element
One document with tags joined into a string
One document with a flattened tags array
One document with fields tags.0 to tags.2
$unwind emits a copy of the document for each array element, with tags set to that single element.
Why should $match usually appear as early as possible in a MongoDB pipeline?
So indexes can be used and fewer documents reach later stages
Because $match must be the first stage of a pipeline by syntax
Because $group cannot run unless a $match comes before it
Because $match results are cached between pipeline runs
A $match at the start can use indexes and shrinks the data every later stage processes. It is not required to be first.
Which MongoDB aggregation stage performs a left outer join with another collection?
$lookup
$unionWith
$merge
$facet
$lookup adds matching documents from another collection as an array. $unionWith appends documents, and $merge writes results to a collection.
A collection has a compound index { a: 1, b: 1 }. Which query can use this index through its prefix?
find({ a: 5 })
find({ b: 5 })
find({ c: 5 })
find({ b: { $gt: 1 } })
A compound index supports queries on its prefixes: a, or a and b. A query only on b cannot use the index for efficient lookup.
explain() for a MongoDB query shows a COLLSCAN stage. What does that mean?
No index was used; every document was scanned
The query was covered by an index
The collection is sharded across several nodes
The plan was taken from the plan cache
COLLSCAN is a full collection scan. Adding a suitable index usually changes it to IXSCAN.
Which MongoDB index type automatically deletes documents after a period based on a date field?
TTL index
Sparse index
Partial index
Hashed index
A TTL index on a Date field with expireAfterSeconds lets a background task remove expired documents, roughly once a minute.
You create a collection with validationAction: "warn" and a $jsonSchema validator. What happens when an insert violates the schema?
The document is inserted and a warning is logged
The insert is rejected with an error
The invalid fields are removed
The document goes to a quarantine collection
With validationAction warn, MongoDB logs violations but accepts the write. The default action, error, rejects invalid documents.
In a three-member MongoDB replica set, the primary crashes. What happens next?
The remaining members elect a new primary
Writes queue on secondaries until it returns
Every secondary starts accepting writes
The set stays read-only until an admin acts
The two remaining members still form a majority, so they hold an election and promote a secondary, usually within seconds.
What does writeConcern { w: "majority" } guarantee in a MongoDB replica set?
The write is acknowledged after most voting members have it
The write is copied to a majority of the shards in the cluster
The write is retried until most connected clients see it
The write is acknowledged once it is on the primary only
Majority write concern waits until a majority of voting members have applied the write, so it survives a failover and will not be rolled back.
Why is a monotonically increasing shard key, such as a timestamp, a poor choice with ranged sharding?
All new inserts go to one shard, creating a hot spot
MongoDB cannot use range sharding on date or time fields
Chunks can no longer be split or moved between shards
Queries by timestamp must be sent to every shard
With ranged sharding, increasing values always fall into the last chunk, so one shard takes all writes. Hashed or compound keys spread them.
In a sharded MongoDB cluster, which component routes client queries to the right shards?
The mongos router
The config servers
An arbiter node
The first shard's primary
Clients connect to mongos, which uses metadata from the config servers to route each operation to the shards that own the data.
Starting with which MongoDB version are multi-document ACID transactions supported on replica sets?
MongoDB 4.0 added multi-document transactions on replica sets, and 4.2 extended them to sharded clusters.
Without an explicit transaction, is an update that changes several fields of one MongoDB document atomic?
Yes, writes to a single document are atomic
No, each field is updated separately
Only if the document is under 1 MB
Only if the changed fields are indexed
MongoDB guarantees atomicity at the single-document level, including embedded documents. Transactions are only needed across documents.
What happens when a MongoDB capped collection reaches its size limit and you insert a new document?
The oldest documents are overwritten
The insert fails with an error
The collection doubles its size
The new document is silently rejected
Capped collections work like a circular buffer: they keep insertion order and remove the oldest documents to make room.
Which collection option enforces JSON Schema rules on MongoDB inserts and updates?
validator with $jsonSchema
schema with $jsonSchema
enforce with $types
rules with $validate
db.createCollection(name, { validator: { $jsonSchema: {...} } }) defines schema validation, which can also be added later with collMod.
redis: Which Redis data type fits a game leaderboard ranked by score?
Sorted Set
List
Hash
HyperLogLog
A Sorted Set keeps members ordered by score, so ZADD, ZINCRBY and ZREVRANGE give rankings directly. HyperLogLog only estimates how many distinct items there are.
Key counter holds the string "10". What does INCR counter return in Redis?
An error
INCR parses a string that holds an integer, adds one and stores the result, so it returns 11. It errors only when the value is not an integer.
In Redis you run LPUSH mylist a b c. What does LRANGE mylist 0 -1 return?
c, b, a
a, b, c
b, c, a
a, c, b
LPUSH inserts each value at the head in order, so c ends up first. RPUSH would keep a, b, c.
Which Redis command sets a field inside a Hash, such as the email of user:42?
HSET
SADD
ZADD
LSET
HSET user:42 email a@b.kz sets one field of the hash. LSET changes a list element by index.
In Redis you run SADD tags x x y. What does SCARD tags return?
A Set stores unique members, so the duplicate x is ignored and the set has two members.
In Redis you run EXPIRE session 60, then SET session newvalue with no options. What happens to the TTL?
It is removed, so the key no longer expires
The original 60 seconds keep counting down as before
It resets to a fresh 60 seconds from the SET
SET fails because the key still has a TTL set
A plain SET discards any existing TTL. Use SET with KEEPTTL (Redis 6.0+) or EX to keep or set one.
What does the Redis TTL command return for an existing key that has no expiration?
nil
TTL returns -1 for a key without an expiry and -2 when the key does not exist.
Redis has maxmemory set and maxmemory-policy noeviction (the default). What happens when memory is full?
Writes that need more memory return an error
The least recently used keys are deleted
Random keys that have a TTL are deleted
Redis swaps data out to disk
With noeviction, Redis refuses commands that would use more memory and keeps serving reads. Eviction only happens with another policy.
Redis is used as a pure cache and many keys have no TTL. Which maxmemory-policy evicts the least recently used keys among all keys?
allkeys-lru
volatile-lru
noeviction
volatile-ttl
The volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL, so here they would barely free memory. allkeys-lru considers every key.
Which Redis persistence option logs every write command and usually loses less data on a crash?
AOF (append-only file)
RDB snapshots
The replication backlog
Keyspace notifications
AOF appends each write and replays it on restart. RDB saves point-in-time snapshots, so writes since the last snapshot can be lost.
Redis AOF is configured with appendfsync everysec. What is the durability trade-off?
About one second of writes can be lost on a crash
The AOF file is fully rewritten once every second
An RDB snapshot is taken every second alongside it
Every write is fsynced before Redis replies to it
everysec fsyncs once per second, balancing speed and safety. appendfsync always fsyncs every write but is much slower.
How does Redis create an RDB snapshot with BGSAVE without blocking clients?
It forks a child process that writes the snapshot
It pauses all clients while the file is written
It streams the data to a replica, which writes it
It writes only the keys that changed since server startup
The child uses copy-on-write memory to write a consistent snapshot while the parent keeps serving requests.
A Redis Pub/Sub subscriber disconnects for a minute and reconnects. What happens to messages published meanwhile?
They are lost, Pub/Sub stores nothing
They are delivered after it resubscribes
They are kept for the channel's TTL
They are replayed from the AOF file
Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: only currently connected subscribers receive messages. Redis Streams provide durable, replayable messaging.
A Redis client runs PSUBSCRIBE news.*. Which messages does it receive?
Messages on channels like news.sport and news.tech
Only messages on the literal channel news.*
Changes to keys whose names start with news.
Only the last message on each channel
PSUBSCRIBE subscribes to channel name patterns using glob-style matching. Key changes are only sent through keyspace notifications.
What is the main job of Redis Sentinel?
Monitoring a primary and promoting a replica if it fails
Splitting keys across several primaries by hash slot
Encrypting all traffic between clients and the Redis server
Compressing RDB files before they are backed up
Sentinel provides high availability for non-clustered Redis: monitoring, notification and automatic failover. Sharding by hash slot is Redis Cluster.
How many hash slots does Redis Cluster divide the keyspace into?
Each key maps to one of 16384 slots via CRC16(key) mod 16384, and slots are assigned to primaries.
In Redis Cluster, MSET user1:name A user1:age 20 fails with a CROSSSLOT error. What is the standard fix?
Use hash tags such as {user1}:name and {user1}:age
Run CLUSTER RESET on each node before the command
Wrap the command in MULTI and EXEC so it is atomic
Switch the client to the RESP3 protocol and retry
Only the part inside braces is hashed, so keys sharing {user1} land in the same slot and multi-key commands work.
What is the main benefit of Redis pipelining?
Fewer network round trips by batching commands
Making the batch of commands atomic
Running commands in parallel on many cores
Compressing commands to save bandwidth
The client sends many commands without waiting for each reply. A pipeline is not atomic; other clients' commands can interleave.
Inside a Redis MULTI/EXEC block, one command fails at runtime (for example INCR on a list). What happens?
The other commands still run; nothing is rolled back
All commands in the block are rolled back together
EXEC returns nil and none of the commands run
Redis retries the failed command once, then aborts
Redis transactions do not support rollback. Runtime errors are returned for that command only; EXEC returns nil only when a WATCHed key changed.
What does WATCH balance do when used before MULTI in Redis?
EXEC aborts if balance changes before it runs
It locks balance so others cannot write it
It streams every change of balance to the client
It delays the expiry of balance during the transaction
WATCH gives optimistic locking: if another client modifies the watched key before EXEC, the transaction is not executed and EXEC returns nil.
cassandra: How is data in a Cassandra table organized?
Rows grouped into partitions by partition key
Rows in one global B-Tree by primary key
BSON documents stored in collections
Each column stored in its own file
Cassandra is a wide-column store: the partition key decides which partition (and nodes) a row belongs to, and rows inside a partition are sorted by clustering columns.
A Cassandra table has PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at). What is the partition key?
user_id
created_at
user_id, created_at
No partition key
The first element of the primary key (in the inner parentheses) is the partition key. created_at is a clustering column.
What does a clustering column do in a Cassandra table?
Sets the sort order of rows within a partition
Decides which node stores the partition
Sets the replication factor of the table
Creates a secondary index on the column
Clustering columns order rows on disk inside each partition, which makes range queries and ORDER BY on them efficient. Node placement comes from the partition key.
A table has PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts). Which query works without ALLOW FILTERING?
WHERE sensor_id = ? AND day = ? AND ts > ?
WHERE sensor_id = ? AND ts > ? AND ts < ?
WHERE day = ? AND ts > ? AND ts < ?
WHERE sensor_id IN (?) AND ts > ?
Cassandra must know the full partition key (sensor_id and day) to locate the partition. Then a range on the clustering column ts is allowed.
Why do Cassandra time-series models often add a time bucket, such as day, to the partition key?
To keep partitions from growing without bound
To allow joins between different tables
Because two partition key columns are required
To make all writes synchronous
A partition per sensor would grow forever. Bucketing by day keeps each partition a manageable size.
With replication factor 3, writes and reads both use QUORUM. Why do reads see the latest write?
2 + 2 > 3, so the read and write replica sets overlap
QUORUM waits for all three replicas to answer
QUORUM always reads from the coordinator node itself
QUORUM locks the row during the write until reads end
When R + W > RF, at least one replica in every read has the latest write, and the newest timestamp wins.
In Cassandra, how many replicas must acknowledge a write at consistency level ONE?
One replica
Two replicas
All replicas
A quorum of replicas
ONE returns success after a single replica acknowledges. It gives the lowest latency but the weakest consistency.
Which Cassandra consistency level requires a quorum only within the coordinator's data center, avoiding cross-DC latency?
LOCAL_QUORUM
EACH_QUORUM
QUORUM
LOCAL_ONE
LOCAL_QUORUM counts replicas in the local DC only. QUORUM counts across all DCs, and EACH_QUORUM needs a quorum in every DC.
A Cassandra keyspace has replication factor 3 on a 6-node cluster. What does that mean?
Each row is stored on three nodes
Each row is split into three pieces
Three nodes act as masters
Every write needs three acknowledgments
RF is the number of copies of each partition. How many replicas must acknowledge is set separately by the consistency level.
Which Cassandra replication strategy should a production keyspace spanning several data centers use?
NetworkTopologyStrategy
SimpleStrategy
LocalStrategy
MultiDatacenterStrategy
NetworkTopologyStrategy sets a replication factor per DC and is rack-aware. SimpleStrategy ignores topology and is meant for single-DC testing.
With replication factor 3 and QUORUM reads and writes, one replica node goes down. What happens to requests for its data?
They still succeed, as two of three replicas respond
They fail until the down node comes back and is repaired
Only reads succeed until the node returns
Only writes succeed until the node returns
QUORUM with RF 3 needs 2 replicas, so one failure is tolerated. Hinted handoff and repair later catch the node up.
In Cassandra, how do you usually serve a query that needs data from two entities?
Model a denormalized table designed for that query
Use a JOIN between the two tables in a CQL query
Use a foreign key between the tables with ON DELETE CASCADE
Use a subquery on the second table in the WHERE clause
CQL has no joins or foreign keys. Cassandra data modeling starts from queries and duplicates data into query-specific tables.
In Cassandra, what happens when you INSERT a row whose primary key already exists?
It overwrites the existing values without an error
It fails with a duplicate primary key error
It creates a second row that has the very same primary key
It is ignored unless the IF EXISTS clause is used
INSERT and UPDATE are both upserts in Cassandra. Values with the newer timestamp win.
Which CQL clause makes an INSERT succeed only when the row does not exist yet?
IF NOT EXISTS
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
WHERE NOT EXISTS
USING UNIQUE
IF NOT EXISTS turns the insert into a lightweight transaction based on Paxos. It is slower than a normal write. ON CONFLICT is PostgreSQL syntax.
When a write arrives at a Cassandra replica, what happens first?
It is appended to the commit log and written to a memtable
It is written straight into an existing SSTable on disk
It is merged right away into the largest SSTable on the disk
It is placed in the compaction queue until the next run
The commit log gives durability and the memtable is an in-memory structure. Memtables are later flushed to new SSTables.
What happens to a Cassandra SSTable after it has been written to disk?
It is never modified; changes go to newer SSTables
It is edited in place each time a row is updated
It is deleted after the next read of its data
It is loaded back into a memtable for every change
SSTables are immutable. Reads merge data from the memtable and several SSTables, and compaction later combines them.
What does a DELETE in Cassandra actually write?
A tombstone that compaction purges later
An immediate removal from every SSTable
A lock on the row until repair runs
A new empty memtable for the table
Because SSTables are immutable, deletes are markers. Tombstones are removed by compaction after gc_grace_seconds.
What is the main purpose of compaction in Cassandra?
Merging SSTables and discarding obsolete data
Compressing commit log segments on disk
Rebalancing token ranges between nodes
Copying data to new replicas after a node failure
Compaction merges SSTables, keeps the newest version of each cell and removes expired tombstones, which reduces the number of files a read must check.
Which compaction strategy is recommended for time-series data written in time order and expired with TTL?
TimeWindowCompactionStrategy
SizeTieredCompactionStrategy
LeveledCompactionStrategy
DateTieredCompactionStrategy
TWCS groups SSTables by time window so whole expired windows can be dropped cheaply. DateTieredCompactionStrategy is deprecated in favor of TWCS.
What does running nodetool repair do in Cassandra?
Synchronizes data between replicas to fix inconsistencies
Rebuilds corrupted SSTables from the commit log on disk
Changes the replication factor of a keyspace on all nodes
Removes a dead node from the ring and its token ranges
Anti-entropy repair compares replicas using Merkle trees and streams missing data. It should run regularly, within gc_grace_seconds.
clickhouse: Why is SELECT avg(price) FROM sales fast in ClickHouse even when sales has 200 columns?
Only the price column is read from disk
The whole row is cached in RAM
ClickHouse precomputes all averages
Rows are sorted by price on insert
In columnar storage each column lives in its own files, so the query reads just the column it needs.
Which workload is a poor fit for ClickHouse?
Many small single-row updates per second
Aggregating billions of log rows
Scanning a few columns of a wide table
Batch-loading daily event files
ClickHouse is built for analytics on large, mostly append-only data. Frequent point updates are expensive because data parts are immutable.
What does the ORDER BY clause of a MergeTree table define?
The sort order in parts and, by default, the primary index
A uniqueness constraint enforced on those columns
The order of rows returned by every SELECT on the table
How the table's data is split across the cluster's shards
Rows in each part are sorted by ORDER BY, and the sparse primary index is built from it unless PRIMARY KEY is set separately. It does not enforce uniqueness.
You insert two rows with the same primary key into a plain MergeTree table. What happens?
Both rows are stored
The second insert fails
The second replaces the first
Only the larger row is kept
The MergeTree primary key is for sorting and data skipping, not uniqueness. Deduplication needs an engine like ReplacingMergeTree.
When does ReplacingMergeTree remove rows with the same sorting key?
During background merges, at no guaranteed time
At insert time, by rejecting the duplicate
Right after each INSERT statement commits
Whenever any SELECT reads the table
Deduplication happens only when parts merge, so queries may still see duplicates. Use FINAL or GROUP BY when exact results matter.
Which ClickHouse engine sums numeric columns of rows with the same sorting key during merges?
SummingMergeTree
CollapsingMergeTree
ReplacingMergeTree
GraphiteMergeTree
SummingMergeTree adds up numeric columns of rows with equal sorting keys when parts merge. GraphiteMergeTree rolls up Graphite metrics by retention rules.
Which column type stores partial aggregate states for an AggregatingMergeTree table?
AggregateFunction
LowCardinality
Nullable(Float64)
Array(Float64)
AggregateFunction(uniq, UInt64) stores intermediate states written with -State functions and read back with -Merge functions such as uniqMerge.
What is the default index_granularity of a MergeTree table (rows per primary index mark)?
The sparse primary index stores one mark per granule of 8192 rows by default, which keeps the index small enough for memory.
In open-source ClickHouse server with default settings, which compression codec does MergeTree use for columns?
LZ4
ZSTD
Gzip
Snappy
LZ4 is the default because it decompresses very fast. ZSTD can be set per column or in server settings for a better ratio.
Which ClickHouse codec stores the differences between consecutive values, which suits slowly increasing timestamps?
Delta
Gorilla
LZ4HC
ZSTD
Delta (or DoubleDelta) turns increasing values into small numbers that then compress well with LZ4 or ZSTD. Gorilla targets floating-point gauges.
Why does columnar data usually compress better than row-oriented data?
Values in one column share a type and look alike
Rows are encrypted before they are compressed
Columns are stored as JSON text, which packs well
Each value gets its own dictionary for encoding
Neighboring values of the same column are homogeneous and often repetitive, so general and specialized codecs reach high ratios.
What does vectorized query execution mean in ClickHouse?
Processing column values in blocks, not row by row
Running every query on the GPU as vector math
Storing each row as an embedding vector
Sending one row at a time to each thread
Operators work on blocks of column data, which cuts per-row overhead and lets the CPU use caches and SIMD efficiently.
Which CPU feature does vectorized execution in ClickHouse mainly exploit?
SIMD instructions
Hyper-threading only
Hardware transactional memory
Virtualization extensions
SIMD (such as SSE and AVX) applies one instruction to many values at once, which fits tight loops over column blocks.
What is a table with the Distributed engine in ClickHouse?
A proxy over local tables on shards, storing no data
A table that copies all data to every node
A table that keeps its data in ZooKeeper
A table that caches the results of remote queries on disk
A Distributed table forwards queries to local tables on each shard and merges the results. The data itself lives in the local MergeTree tables.
Which ClickHouse engine keeps the replicas of a shard in sync?
ReplicatedMergeTree
Distributed
ReplacingMergeTree
CollapsingMergeTree
Replicated*MergeTree engines coordinate replicas through ClickHouse Keeper or ZooKeeper. Distributed only routes queries to shards, and Replacing or Collapsing engines deduplicate rows locally.
When you insert into a Distributed table that spans several shards, what decides each row's target shard?
The sharding key in the table definition
The first column of the table's ORDER BY
The node that has the most free disk space
The PARTITION BY expression of the table
The Distributed engine evaluates the sharding key (for example rand() or cityHash64(user_id)) and uses shard weights to route each row.
What usually causes a 'Too many parts' error in ClickHouse?
Many tiny inserts creating parts faster than merges
Too many concurrent SELECT queries on the same table
Too many data skipping indexes on one table
Too many columns defined in a single table
Each INSERT creates at least one new part. Many small inserts outrun background merges until ClickHouse throttles or rejects writes.
An app sends 1000 single-row INSERTs per second to ClickHouse. What is the best fix?
Batch rows client-side or enable async_insert
Add more columns to the ORDER BY key of the table
Switch the table to the Log engine for speed
Run OPTIMIZE TABLE after every insert
ClickHouse prefers fewer, larger inserts (thousands of rows or more). async_insert lets the server buffer small inserts into larger parts.
Which ClickHouse function gives a fast approximate count of distinct values?
uniq
uniqExact
count
groupArray
uniq uses an adaptive sampling algorithm with small memory use. uniqExact is precise but needs memory proportional to the number of distinct values.
A ClickHouse dashboard repeatedly aggregates raw events by hour and is slow. Which feature fits best?
A materialized view that pre-aggregates on insert
A larger index_granularity setting on the raw table
A Distributed table defined over a single shard
A Buffer table in front of the raw table
A materialized view can write hourly aggregates into a SummingMergeTree or AggregatingMergeTree table as data arrives, so the dashboard reads far fewer rows.
duckdb: How does DuckDB run?
In-process inside the host application, with no server
As a cluster of nodes managed by a coordinator node
As a cloud warehouse that clients access over REST
As a background daemon that clients reach over TCP
DuckDB is an embedded library, like SQLite, but optimized for analytics. It runs inside Python, R, a CLI or another app.
In Python, what does duckdb.connect() with no arguments create?
An in-memory database lost when the process ends
A file named duckdb.db in the current folder
A connection to a shared server instance
An error, because a path is required
The default database is :memory:. Pass a file path to persist data.
How does a persistent DuckDB database store its data?
In a single database file
As a folder of Parquet files
Inside an SQLite file
As one CSV file per table
DuckDB uses its own single-file storage format, similar in spirit to SQLite but columnar.
Can two separate processes write to the same DuckDB database file at the same time?
No, only one process can open it read-write
Yes, using row-level locks across processes
Yes, but only on Linux file systems
Yes, once WAL mode is enabled
DuckDB allows one read-write process, or several read-only processes. Threads within that one process can write concurrently.
Why does DuckDB's vectorized engine aggregate faster than a row-at-a-time engine?
It processes batches of column values, cutting per-row overhead
It precomputes all aggregates when the data is first loaded
It sends each row to a separate thread for processing
It stores every column as a B-Tree index for fast lookups
Operators handle vectors of values at once, which keeps data in CPU caches and reduces interpretation overhead.
Which DuckDB statement sets the number of CPU threads it uses?
SET threads = 4
SET cores = 4
SET parallelism = 4
SET max_cpus = 4
DuckDB uses all available cores by default, and the threads setting limits or raises that.
What does SELECT count(*) FROM 'events/*.parquet' do in DuckDB?
Counts rows across all matching Parquet files
Fails, since files must be imported first
Counts the number of matching files
Counts rows in the first matching file only
DuckDB can query Parquet, CSV and JSON files in place, and glob patterns combine many files into one table.
Which DuckDB function reads a CSV file and auto-detects the delimiter, header and column types?
read_csv('file.csv')
load_csv('file.csv')
import_csv('file.csv')
csv_scan('file.csv')
read_csv uses a CSV sniffer to detect the dialect and types. You can also simply write FROM 'file.csv'.
Why is SELECT a FROM 'big.parquet' much faster in DuckDB than SELECT * FROM 'big.parquet' on a wide file?
Only column a's data is read from the file
Parquet files are cached after one query
DuckDB builds an index on column a first
SELECT * decompresses the whole file twice
Parquet is columnar, so DuckDB uses projection pushdown to read just the needed column chunks. Filters can also skip row groups.
Which DuckDB statement writes query results to a Parquet file?
COPY (SELECT * FROM t) TO 'out.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)
EXPORT t INTO PARQUET 'out.parquet' WITH (FORMAT parquet)
SAVE (SELECT * FROM t) AS 'out.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)
INSERT INTO 'out.parquet' SELECT * FROM t (FORMAT parquet)
COPY ... TO with FORMAT parquet writes the result of a query or table. FORMAT csv and json work the same way.
Which DuckDB query is valid shorthand for SELECT * FROM tbl?
FROM tbl
GET tbl
READ tbl
ROWS tbl
DuckDB supports FROM-first syntax, and a bare FROM tbl returns all columns.
In DuckDB, what does SELECT * EXCLUDE (password) FROM users return?
All columns except password
Only the password column
Rows where password is NULL
An error, EXCLUDE is not valid
EXCLUDE is a DuckDB extension to star expressions. REPLACE is a related one that swaps in an expression for a column.
What does GROUP BY ALL do in DuckDB?
Groups by every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list
Puts all rows of the table into one single group
Groups by every column of the table, aggregated or not
Keeps NULL groups that GROUP BY normally drops
GROUP BY ALL infers the grouping columns from the SELECT list, so you do not have to repeat them.
Which workload fits DuckDB worst?
Many concurrent small writes from many app clients
Aggregating a 10 GB Parquet dataset on a single laptop
Joining CSV exports inside a notebook
Running analytics in a Python ETL script
DuckDB is an OLAP engine for one process. High-concurrency transactional workloads from many clients suit an OLTP server like PostgreSQL.
Which statement best compares DuckDB with SQLite?
DuckDB is columnar for analytics; SQLite is row-based for OLTP
DuckDB is a client-server database; SQLite is embedded
DuckDB is row-based for OLTP; SQLite is columnar for analytics
DuckDB requires a schema server; SQLite does not need one
Both are embedded single-file databases. DuckDB targets scans and aggregations, while SQLite targets point reads and small transactions.
A pandas DataFrame df exists in your Python scope. How do you query it with DuckDB?
duckdb.sql('SELECT * FROM df')
duckdb.load(df).sql('SELECT *')
duckdb.sql('SELECT * FROM pandas.df')
df.duckdb.sql('SELECT *')
DuckDB's replacement scans find Python variables by name, so a DataFrame can be queried directly without copying it into a table first.
Which method turns a DuckDB relation in Python into a pandas DataFrame?
.df()
.frame()
.as_pandas()
.to_table()
duckdb.sql('...').df() returns a pandas DataFrame. Related methods include .pl() for Polars and .arrow() for Arrow.
Why can DuckDB query a large Apache Arrow table in Python with very little overhead?
It reads Arrow's columnar buffers without copying them
It converts Arrow tables to CSV first, which is quick
It uploads the table to a local DuckDB server process first
It samples only 10 percent of the rows by default
DuckDB and Arrow are both columnar, so DuckDB scans Arrow memory directly (zero-copy) and can push down filters and projections.
Which R call opens an in-memory DuckDB connection through DBI?
dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())
duckdb_open(memory = TRUE)
DBI::duckConnect()
The duckdb R package provides a DBI driver, so standard DBI functions like dbGetQuery work. dplyr can also use it via dbplyr.
Which DuckDB extension lets it read Parquet files directly from S3 or HTTPS URLs?
httpfs
json
fts
spatial
httpfs adds HTTP(S) and S3 file system support. Recent DuckDB versions can autoload it when you query a remote path.
snowflake: Which three layers make up Snowflake's architecture?
Database storage, query processing and cloud services
Ingestion, indexing and reporting service layers
Master nodes, worker nodes and coordinator pools
Row store, column store and query result cache
Storage holds data centrally, virtual warehouses process queries, and the cloud services layer handles metadata, security and optimization.
What does Snowflake's separation of storage and compute let you do?
Scale or pause compute without moving data
Avoid paying for storage entirely
Share CPU with the warehouses of other accounts
Keep indexes on separate disks
All warehouses read the same central storage, so compute can be resized, added or suspended independently of the data.
Two teams run heavy queries on one Snowflake warehouse and slow each other down. What is the typical fix?
Give each team its own virtual warehouse
Copy the tables into a second database
Add indexes to the shared tables
Increase the Time Travel retention
Warehouses are isolated compute clusters over the same data, so separate warehouses remove contention without duplicating data.
Many users run queries at the same time and queries queue, but each query is fast on its own. Which Snowflake feature helps most?
A multi-cluster warehouse that adds clusters
Resizing the warehouse from Medium up to X-Large
A clustering key defined on the main table
A longer AUTO_SUSPEND period for the warehouse
Scaling out with more clusters targets concurrency. Scaling up to a larger size mainly speeds up individual heavy queries.
What does AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 do on a Snowflake warehouse?
Suspends it after 60 seconds of inactivity
Cancels any query that runs over 60 seconds
Resumes it every 60 seconds
Limits it to 60 credits per day
An idle warehouse suspends to stop consuming credits. AUTO_RESUME restarts it when a new query arrives.
What happens when you resize a Snowflake warehouse from Small to Medium?
Its compute doubles, and so do its credits per hour
The amount of data it is able to query doubles
It can store twice as much table data as before
Its credits per hour stay exactly the same as before
Each size step doubles the compute resources and the credit rate. Storage is independent of warehouse size.
How does Snowflake physically store table data?
In immutable, compressed columnar micro-partitions
In B-Tree indexes that the user defines per table
In row-oriented pages on the local disks of nodes
In one compressed file per table for each day of data
Data is automatically split into micro-partitions (roughly 50 to 500 MB uncompressed) stored in columnar form, with metadata about each.
Why can WHERE event_date = '2024-05-01' be fast in Snowflake without any indexes?
Min and max metadata per micro-partition lets it skip partitions
Snowflake builds a hash index on every date column automatically
Results always come from the query result cache for date filters
Dates are kept in a separate lookup table that is joined first
Snowflake keeps value ranges for every column in each micro-partition and prunes those that cannot match the filter.
When does defining a clustering key on a Snowflake table usually make sense?
On very large tables whose common filters prune poorly
On every table, right after creating it, as a best practice
On small lookup tables that only have a few rows
On tables that are used only for full table scans
Automatic clustering costs credits, so it pays off on multi-terabyte tables where natural load order does not match query filters.
What does SELECT * FROM orders AT(OFFSET => -3600) return in Snowflake?
The table as it was one hour ago
Only rows changed in the last hour
Rows inserted more than one hour ago
The table one hour after the next load
Time Travel's AT clause queries historical data at a timestamp, an offset in seconds, or a statement ID.
Which Snowflake command restores a table dropped within its Time Travel retention period?
UNDROP TABLE orders
RESTORE TABLE orders
RECOVER TABLE orders
ROLLBACK TABLE orders
UNDROP works for tables, schemas and databases while their data is still in Time Travel.
What is Fail-safe in Snowflake?
A 7-day period where only Snowflake can recover data
A setting that blocks DROP statements on important tables
A read-only replica users query during outages
An extra Time Travel window users can query
After Time Travel ends, permanent tables enter a 7-day Fail-safe period. Users cannot query it; Snowflake support can recover data in disasters.
What is the default DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS (Time Travel) for a permanent Snowflake table?
The default is 1 day. Enterprise edition and higher can raise it up to 90 days for permanent tables.
What is a stage in Snowflake?
A location of data files for loading or unloading
A single step in a query's execution plan profile
A temporary virtual warehouse used only for loads
A sandbox copy of a production database for tests
Stages are internal (Snowflake-managed) or external (S3, GCS, Azure). COPY INTO loads from them and unloads to them.
Which syntax refers to the current user's internal stage in Snowflake?
@%orders
@~ is the user stage, @%table_name is a table stage, and @name refers to a named stage.
You run COPY INTO t FROM @s twice on the same unchanged files. What happens on the second run?
Files already loaded are skipped
Every row is loaded a second time
The command fails with a duplicate error
The table is truncated and reloaded
Snowflake keeps load metadata per table for 64 days and skips files it already loaded, unless FORCE = TRUE is used.
What is Snowpipe used for?
Loading files soon after they land in a stage
Streaming query results out to BI tools in real time
Replicating databases across cloud regions
Scheduling SQL tasks to run on a cron
Snowpipe runs serverless, continuous micro-batch loads, usually triggered by cloud storage event notifications.
How does Snowflake Secure Data Sharing give another account access to data?
It grants read access to the provider's data without a copy
It exports the data as files that the consumer loads
It copies the tables into the consumer account's storage
It sends a signed snapshot of the database to the consumer
Shares expose objects through metadata only. Consumers query live data, and no storage is duplicated.
A consumer with its own full Snowflake account queries a database shared with it. Who pays for the compute of those queries?
The consumer, through its own warehouse
The provider that created the share
Both accounts split the cost equally
Nobody, since shared queries are free
Consumers run queries on their own warehouses. Providers pay only for storage, and for compute in reader accounts they create.
What happens to storage right after CREATE TABLE dev_orders CLONE orders in Snowflake?
Nothing is copied; both tables share micro-partitions
All data is duplicated into new storage
Only the schema is copied; the clone starts out empty
The clone stays read-only until a refresh
Zero-copy cloning only copies metadata. New storage is used only for micro-partitions that change later in either table.
bigquery: In BigQuery's default on-demand model, what must you provision before running a query?
Nothing, compute is allocated automatically
A cluster of worker virtual machines
A virtual warehouse of a chosen size
A dedicated database server instance
BigQuery is serverless: Google allocates slots per query, and you only create datasets and tables.
What does BigQuery on-demand pricing charge queries for?
Bytes processed by the query
Rows returned to the client
Wall-clock run time of the query
Number of tables joined
On-demand queries are billed by the bytes read from the referenced columns. Capacity pricing instead bills reserved slots.
Does adding LIMIT 10 reduce the bytes billed for SELECT * on a non-clustered BigQuery table?
No, all selected columns are still scanned
Yes, only the first 10 rows are read
Yes, only the first partition is read
Yes, bytes billed drop by about 90 percent
LIMIT is applied after scanning, so cost depends on selected columns and pruning. Use column selection, partition filters or table preview instead.
A BigQuery table is partitioned on its DATE column event_date. Which query clause enables partition pruning?
WHERE event_date = '2024-05-01'
WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY event_date
WHERE country = 'KZ' GROUP BY event_date
ORDER BY event_date LIMIT 100
Only filters on the partitioning column let BigQuery skip partitions. Sorting with LIMIT still scans every partition.
Which BigQuery table option rejects queries that do not filter on the partition column?
require_partition_filter = TRUE
partition_expiration_days = 1
enforce_partition_pruning = TRUE
max_staleness = INTERVAL 1 DAY
require_partition_filter protects large partitioned tables from accidental full scans. partition_expiration_days deletes old partitions, and max_staleness controls cached freshness.
What does clustering a BigQuery table by customer_id mainly improve?
Filters and aggregations on customer_id read fewer blocks
Every customer_id value stored in the table becomes unique
Inserts into the table become free of any charge
Joins on all other columns of the table get faster
Clustering sorts data within storage blocks, so BigQuery can skip blocks that cannot match filters on the clustered columns.
How many clustering columns can a BigQuery table have at most?
BigQuery allows up to four clustering columns, and their order matters, like a composite index.
What is a slot in BigQuery?
A unit of virtual CPU and memory for running queries
A storage block that holds 1 GB of table data
A reserved name for a temporary results table
A concurrent user session open in the BigQuery web console
Queries are split into stages run by many slots in parallel. Reservations buy a fixed number of slots.
What is the name of the distributed query engine behind BigQuery?
Dremel
Spanner
Bigtable
Borg
BigQuery runs on Dremel for execution, Colossus for storage and the Jupiter network for shuffles. Borg is Google's cluster manager.
A team runs heavy, steady BigQuery workloads all day and wants predictable cost. Which pricing model fits?
Capacity pricing with slot reservations
On-demand pricing based on the bytes scanned
Streaming insert pricing per row
Long-term storage pricing for tables
Capacity (slot-based) pricing charges for reserved compute regardless of bytes scanned, which suits constant heavy usage.
You rerun an identical BigQuery query within 24 hours, and the tables have not changed. What usually happens?
Cached results are returned at no charge
The query is billed again at full price
The query fails as a duplicate
Results are returned only for new rows
BigQuery caches query results for about 24 hours. Cached results are not billed, unless caching is disabled or the query is non-deterministic.
What does UNNEST do with an ARRAY column in BigQuery?
Turns array elements into rows
Joins elements into one string
Removes NULL elements from the array
Converts the array into a STRUCT
UNNEST produces a table with one row per element, which you can join, filter or aggregate.
What does SELECT o.id, item.sku FROM orders o, UNNEST(o.items) AS item return in BigQuery?
One row per item of each order
One row per order with items as a list
Only orders that have exactly one item
Only the first item of each order
The comma is a correlated cross join with the order's own array. Orders with empty arrays drop out unless you use LEFT JOIN UNNEST.
In BigQuery, how do you select field city from a STRUCT column named address?
address.city
address['city']
address->city
address::city
STRUCT fields are accessed with dot notation. The -> and :: operators are PostgreSQL syntax.
Why does BigQuery recommend nested and repeated fields for orders and their line items?
They avoid costly joins by storing related data together
They are required before a table can be partitioned
They make each column of the table nullable by default instead
They raise the project's slot quota for those queries
Denormalizing into ARRAY of STRUCT keeps line items inside the order row, so queries avoid large shuffling joins.
How can you see how many bytes a BigQuery query will process before running it?
Run it as a dry run
Run it with LIMIT 1 first
Check INFORMATION_SCHEMA
Prefix it with EXPLAIN
A dry run validates the query and returns the estimated bytes processed without billing. The console shows the same estimate.
Which BigQuery job setting makes a query fail instead of processing more bytes than a limit?
Maximum bytes billed
Maximum rows returned
Query timeout in seconds
Slot usage limit
With maximum bytes billed set, a query that would exceed it fails before running and incurs no charge.
What is a BigQuery external table?
A table whose data stays in a source like Cloud Storage
A table that is copied in full each night from Cloud Storage
A table that is stored in another Google account
A view defined over a remote MySQL database
External tables read files (CSV, Parquet, and so on) in place at query time, so no data is loaded into BigQuery storage.
Compared with a native BigQuery table, querying a CSV external table in Cloud Storage is usually:
Slower, because files are parsed at query time
Faster, because no storage format is involved
Identical, since the data is loaded first
Impossible to join with native tables
Native tables use an optimized columnar format with metadata. External CSV files must be read and parsed on each query.
Which BigQuery feature runs a live query against a Cloud SQL database?
Federated queries with EXTERNAL_QUERY
The BigQuery Data Transfer Service
A Cloud Storage external table
A materialized view over Cloud SQL
EXTERNAL_QUERY sends SQL through a connection to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB and returns results as a temporary table. Transfer Service copies data on a schedule.
elasticsearch: What does an inverted index map in Elasticsearch?
Each term to the documents that contain it
Each document to its fields in sorted order
Each shard to the nodes that hold its replicas
Each field to the data type in its mapping
Full-text search looks up query terms in the inverted index to find matching documents quickly, instead of scanning every document.
What tokens does the standard analyzer produce for 'The Quick-Brown fox'?
the, quick, brown, fox
the quick-brown fox
quick, brown, fox
the, quick-brown, fox
The standard tokenizer splits on word boundaries such as spaces and hyphens, and the lowercase filter lowercases. Stop words are not removed by default.
Which Elasticsearch field type fits a status or email value used for exact filters and aggregations?
keyword
text
long
match_only_text
keyword stores the value as a single unanalyzed term, which suits exact matches, sorting and aggregations. text is analyzed for full-text search.
In what order does an Elasticsearch analyzer apply its parts?
Character filters, tokenizer, token filters
Tokenizer, character filters, token filters
Token filters, tokenizer, character filters
Tokenizer, token filters, character filters
Character filters clean the raw text, the tokenizer splits it into tokens, and token filters change, add or remove tokens.
Which Elasticsearch API shows the tokens an analyzer produces for a given string?
_analyze
_explain
_validate
_search
POST _analyze with an analyzer and text returns the tokens, which helps debug why a query does or does not match.
Field title is of type text, and a document has title 'Quick Fox'. What does a term query for 'Quick Fox' on title return?
No hits
The document
An error
All documents
The indexed terms are 'quick' and 'fox', but a term query looks for the exact unanalyzed term 'Quick Fox'. Use a match query for text fields.
In an Elasticsearch bool query, how does a filter clause differ from a must clause?
filter does not affect scoring and can be cached
filter excludes matches instead of including them
must only works on keyword fields
filter only works on numeric fields
Both must match, but filter runs in filter context: no relevance score, so it is faster and cacheable. must_not is the clause that excludes.
Which query finds documents with price from 10 to 20, both inclusive?
{"range": {"price": {"gte": 10, "lte": 20}}}
gte and lte are inclusive bounds, while gt and lt are exclusive, so the second option would skip 10 and 20.
Can you change number_of_shards on an existing Elasticsearch index with a settings update?
No, you reindex or use the split or shrink APIs
Yes, at any time with PUT _settings
Yes, but only while the cluster health is yellow
Yes, after removing all replicas
The primary shard count is fixed at index creation because documents are routed by hash modulo the shard count. number_of_replicas can change any time.
What does setting number_of_replicas to 1 on an Elasticsearch index do?
Keeps one copy of each primary shard on another node
Splits each primary shard into two smaller pieces
Copies the whole index over to a second, remote cluster
Doubles the number of primary shards in the index
Replicas provide failover and extra read capacity. A replica is never placed on the same node as its primary.
A single-node Elasticsearch cluster has an index with number_of_replicas set to 1. What is the cluster health?
yellow
green
red
offline
All primaries are assigned, but the replicas cannot be placed on the same node, so they stay unassigned and the status is yellow.
What does red cluster health mean in Elasticsearch?
At least one primary shard is unassigned
Some replica shards are unassigned
CPU usage is above 90 percent
The cluster has only one node
Red means some data is unavailable for search and indexing. Yellow means only replicas are missing.
Which Elasticsearch aggregation returns a document count for each distinct value of status?
terms
cardinality
histogram
avg
terms creates one bucket per value with doc_count. cardinality only returns an approximate number of distinct values.
A terms aggregation on a text field named status fails by default. What is the usual fix?
Aggregate on the keyword sub-field status.keyword
Increase the size parameter of the terms aggregation
Reduce the index to a single shard and retry
Use a match query instead of the aggregation
Text fields have fielddata disabled by default. Dynamic mapping adds a .keyword sub-field that supports aggregations.
Why set "size": 0 in an Elasticsearch search used only for aggregations?
To skip returning hits and get only aggregations
To run the aggregation over zero shards only
To limit each aggregation to zero buckets
To return hits without computing any relevance scores
size controls how many hits are returned. With 0, Elasticsearch skips fetching documents, which is faster and allows request caching.
You index {"age": "25"} into a new index with default dynamic mapping. What type does age get?
text with a keyword sub-field
long, since the value is numeric
keyword only, with no text field
integer, converted from the string
A JSON string is mapped as text plus a keyword sub-field because numeric detection is off by default. Send 25 without quotes to get long.
How do you change an existing Elasticsearch field from text to keyword?
Create a new index with the new mapping and reindex
Send PUT _mapping with the new field type to the index
Refresh the index after editing the mapping
Change it on the replica shards only
Existing field types cannot be changed because indexed data depends on them. You can only add new fields or sub-fields to a mapping.
What is an index template in Elasticsearch used for?
Auto-applying settings and mappings to new matching indices
Copying documents from one index into another index
Restoring an index and its data from a snapshot
Saving a search query so that dashboards and alerts can reuse it
Templates match index name patterns such as logs-* and apply settings, mappings and aliases when such an index is created.
Which Elasticsearch field type stores embeddings for approximate kNN vector search?
dense_vector
float_array
geo_point
nested
A dense_vector field with indexing enabled supports the knn search option. float_array is not an Elasticsearch type.
Which graph-based algorithm does Elasticsearch use for approximate kNN search on dense_vector fields?
HNSW
IVF-PQ
LSH
k-d tree
Elasticsearch builds Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs via Lucene, trading some accuracy for much faster search than brute force.
supabase: Which database powers every Supabase project?
PostgreSQL
MySQL
MongoDB
CockroachDB
Each Supabase project is a full Postgres database, and Auth, Storage and Realtime are built around it.
Which SQL statement enables the pgvector extension in a Supabase project?
create extension vector;
install extension pgvector;
enable module vector;
alter database add vector;
pgvector is installed under the extension name vector. You can also enable it from the Extensions page of the dashboard.
A Supabase table has Row Level Security enabled and no policies. What does a select with the anon key return?
No rows
All rows
An error
Only public rows
With RLS on, access is denied unless a policy allows it, so the query returns an empty result rather than data.
Which RLS policy expression lets users read only their own rows in a todos table with a user_id column?
using (auth.uid() = user_id)
using (auth.role() = user_id)
with check (true)
using (current_user = 'anon')
auth.uid() returns the ID of the signed-in user from the JWT. A USING clause filters which existing rows are visible.
In a Postgres RLS policy, what does the WITH CHECK clause control?
Which new or updated rows may be written
Which existing rows SELECT can see
Which roles may create new policies
Which columns are sent to the client
USING filters existing rows for reads, updates and deletes. WITH CHECK validates the rows produced by INSERT and UPDATE.
Why must the Supabase service_role key never be shipped in browser code?
It bypasses Row Level Security
It expires after one hour
It only works from server IP addresses
It disables Realtime for the project
The service_role key has full access to the database regardless of policies. Browsers should only use the anon (publishable) key.
Which Supabase Realtime feature streams INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events from database tables to clients?
Postgres Changes
Broadcast
Presence
Edge Functions
Postgres Changes listens to database changes. Broadcast sends ephemeral client messages, and Presence tracks shared online state.
You subscribe to Postgres Changes on a messages table but receive no events. What setup step is commonly missing?
Adding the table to the supabase_realtime publication
Creating a trigger on the table that calls pg_notify
Enabling the pg_cron extension for the database
Turning off RLS on the messages table entirely
Realtime only streams tables included in the supabase_realtime publication. RLS still applies to the events, so it should stay on.
Which Supabase Realtime feature tracks which users are currently online in a channel?
Presence
Broadcast
Postgres Changes
Database Webhooks
Presence keeps a synced state per channel and emits join and leave events, which suits online indicators.
In which language and runtime are Supabase Edge Functions written?
TypeScript on a Deno-based runtime
Python on an AWS Lambda runtime
Go compiled to WebAssembly modules
PL/pgSQL running inside the database
